Upper
up'-pēr
adj. (the higher of two parts; of a room, a millstone, a spring, a door post, a chamber)
Comparative of up, Saxon upp. In the Authorized Version upper almost always stands against a stated nether — the upper springs and the nether springs, the upper millstone and the nether — so that the word is never merely a measurement but always one half of a pair.

Biblical Definition

Upper is a small word that keeps company with large events. The blood of the passover lamb was struck “on the two side posts and on the upper door post of the houses” (Exo 12:7) — three marks, and the upper one over the head of everyone who passed beneath it, so that a household went in and out under the blood. The upper millstone was the turning stone, the one that did the grinding, and the law forbade taking it in pledge because “he taketh a man's life to pledge” (Deu 24:6): a creditor may hold a man's property, but not the instrument by which his household eats. Achsah asked her father for water and received “the upper springs, and the nether springs” (Jos 15:19) — an inheritance measured not in acreage but in water, the whole of a thing rather than the half. And Ahaziah “fell down through a lattice in his upper chamber” (2Ki 1:2) and sent to Baalzebub instead of to the LORD, and died for it. The upper chamber is where the Bible puts its quiet rooms: the widow's loft where Elijah lodged, the room where Christ kept the passover, the room where the hundred and twenty waited. Height in Scripture is never neutral. It is either the place of the blood, the place of the prayer, or the place of the fall.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines upper as higher in place; superior; and the upper millstone as the running or turning stone, the nether being the bedstone.

expand to see more

UPPER, a. Higher in place; as the upper lip; the upper story of a house.

1. Superior; higher in power, dignity or station; as the upper ranks of men.

MILLSTONE, n. A stone used for grinding grain. Millstones are used in pairs; the lower or bedstone lies still, and the upper or runner is turned upon it.

NETHER, a. Lower; lying or being beneath, or in the lower part; opposed to upper.

Key Scripture

Exo 12:7 — "And they shall take of the blood, and strike it on the two side posts and on the upper door post of the houses, wherein they shall eat it."

Deu 24:6 — "No man shall take the nether or the upper millstone to pledge: for he taketh a man's life to pledge."

Jos 15:19 — "Who answered, Give me a blessing; for thou hast given me a south land; give me also springs of water. And he gave her the upper springs, and the nether springs."

2Ki 1:2 — "And Ahaziah fell down through a lattice in his upper chamber that was in Samaria, and was sick: and he sent messengers, and said unto them, Go, enquire of Baalzebub the god of Ekron whether I shall recover of this disease."

Modern Corruption

The upper room has been sentimentalized into a mood; Scripture treats it as a place of covenant business.

expand to see more

The modern devotional imagination has made the upper room a warm and private feeling — an atmosphere of intimacy detached from what actually happened in it. But every upper room in Scripture is a place where something is transacted. The passover is instituted; the Supper is given with the words this is my body and this cup is the new testament in my blood; the eleven wait under a command and are filled. The room is not the point. The covenant enacted in the room is the point, and an upper-room piety that keeps the intimacy while dropping the ordinance has kept the furniture and lost the house.

The principle to recover is that the Authorized Version's ordinary words carry covenant weight. The upper door post is not architectural detail; it is the lintel over which the blood stood between a household and the destroyer. The upper millstone is not agricultural detail; it is the reason a lender may not strip a debtor of the means of life. Read the plain words closely and the law and the gospel are found lying in them.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew 'elyon (H5945), upper, higher, uppermost; rekeb (H7393), the upper riding stone of a mill; Greek anogeon (G508), an upper chamber or loft.

expand to see more

Hebrew 'elyon (H5945) — upper, uppermost, highest; used of the upper pool, the upper gate, and (capitalized) of God Most High.

Hebrew rekeb (H7393) — the running or upper stone of a hand mill; Deuteronomy 24:6, Judges 9:53.

Hebrew mashqowph (H4947) — the lintel or upper door post on which the passover blood was struck; Exodus 12:7, 12:22-23.

Greek anogeon (G508) — an upper room, a loft; Mark 14:15, Luke 22:12, of the room furnished for the Supper.

Greek huperoon (G5253) — the upper chamber; Acts 1:13, 9:37, 20:8.

Usage

"“On the upper door post” — the blood stood over the head of every one who went in."

"“The upper springs, and the nether springs” — a daughter asked, and a father gave the whole."

"“In his upper chamber” — and sent to Ekron rather than to the LORD."
